title: Your favorite cause is not the civil rights movement and neither is mine
gist: Yglesias argues progressives and other advocates should not imitate civil rights movement tactics, because that movement was an extraordinary outlier responding to disenfranchisement and a depolarized, state-centric party system that no longer exists; cautious bipartisan incrementalism fits modern politics.

insights.claim: The civil rights movement is the exception that proves the rule: it was extraordinary rather than typical, so analogies from it to modern causes mostly pattern-match poorly.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Weakens the rhetorical trump card progressives use against moderates in strategy debates.
insights.quote: The civil rights movement is the exception that proves the rule.

insights.claim: Claiming one's own cause, even YIMBY housing reform, has the moral weight of civil rights invites competing claims from every other cause that also sees itself as the modern civil rights movement.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Abundance and housing advocates should pursue ordinary bargaining tactics.

insights.claim: Under normal conditions, most legislative change comes from a frustrating process of bargaining with stakeholders; none of today's main progressive or abundance causes are beyond normal political to-and-fro.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Favors incremental bipartisan bills as the realistic path for policy change.
insights.locator: The slow boring of hard boards

insights.claim: Midcentury American politics had low ideological polarization: in the 83rd House (elected 1952), Southern Democrats and Republicans spread across economic and civil rights dimensions, and Republican Jacob Javits was more liberal than many Democrats.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Historical baseline against today's sorted parties.

insights.claim: Modern Congress is almost fully sorted: members vote with party leadership nearly all the time, and even Jared Golden or Henry Cuellar is not to the right of any Republican, while Susan Collins is more conservative than every Democrat.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Crossover votes are rare, so coalition math depends on party-line control.

insights.claim: Midcentury parties were state-first confederations; today state parties are branches of national organizations, a major institutional shift without any constitutional change, so 1954 tactics do not fit 2026.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Nationalized parties make every risky stance a drag on the whole party agenda.

insights.claim: Under contemporary partisanship, a political risk taken for one issue (health care, climate, abortion) drags on every other issue, so calls for bolder action implicitly demand sacrifice elsewhere, which advocates rarely acknowledge.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Expect cautious messaging by electorally exposed parties; tradeoffs are underpriced in activist demands.

insights.claim: Yglesias's preferred politics (caution, attention to downside risk, non-polarized low-profile bipartisan bills, narrow messaging on small changes) is wildly at odds with how civil rights was won, and he says that is because civil rights was extraordinary.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Signals the Slow Boring strategy: low-salience bipartisan bills such as energy permitting.

insights.claim: In Jim Crow Alabama the electorate was unrepresentative, so white moderates were the extreme left of it and could not deliver change; progress required engaging Northern white opinion to overrule the local system.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Raising salience works when the median national voter is on your side but locals block you.
insights.locator: Democracy (or its absence) is a big deal

insights.claim: Civil rights leaders also used ordinary routes: Civil Rights Acts of 1957 and 1960 preceded 1964, the Voting Rights Act followed in 1965, fair housing came in 1968, and low-key litigation in the 1940s laid groundwork for Brown v. Board of Education.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Even the paradigm movement mixed incremental and confrontational tactics.

insights.claim: Northern white voters' first choice was for government to ignore civil rights, but their second choice was to overturn Jim Crow, which is why confrontational protests like Selma and the Freedom Rides worked for this specific situation.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Tactic effectiveness depends on latent majority opinion.

insights.claim: Discipline mattered: when it broke down in the late 1960s with rioting, the backlash was pretty severe.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Disorder erodes public support for a cause.
insights.locator: It was also undertaken in an extremely disciplined way
